blocks.body: The **Pauli-Y gate** combines the effects of both X (bit flip) and Z (phase flip). It flips |0⟩ to |1⟩ and |1⟩ to |0⟩, but with **imaginary** phase factors. It's the least intuitive of the three Pauli gates, but completes the set needed to describe any single-qubit rotation.
The imaginary numbers i and -i are what distinguish Y from X. They introduce a phase that depends on which state you started in:
Let's see the Y gate applied to |0⟩. The probabilities are identical to the X gate (100% chance of |1⟩), but the statevector has an imaginary component:

blocks.caption: Y|0⟩ = i|1⟩ — same probabilities as X|0⟩ but with phase i

blocks.body: Like X and Z, applying Y twice returns to the original state:
The Y gate performs a **π rotation around the Y-axis**. This takes |0⟩ to |1⟩ via the Y-axis of the Bloch sphere (through the +Y point), as opposed to the X gate which goes through the +X point.

blocks.caption: Interactive: compare Y with X and Z

blocks.body: **Key takeaway:** Y = iXZ. It combines bit flip and phase flip with imaginary coefficients. All three Pauli gates (X, Y, Z) are self-inverse and form a complete basis for single-qubit errors in quantum error correction.
